strengths: Simple, training-free, inference-time planning wrapper that can be combined with any pretrained GCRL policy and any compatible distance signal, requiring no online interaction, extra supervision, or privileged information.

Elegant closed-form value-to-distance mappings for common reward conventions (sparse terminal reward and per-step penalty), which makes the value-derived distance a natural default and avoids hand-crafted metrics.

Strong empirical gains on several genuinely hard long-horizon tasks: pointmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 0.0%->80.9% and GCIQL 0.0%->98.0%, and humanoidmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 4.4%->78.1% (Table 3), with low variance.
Ablations (Figure 4a) support the two main design choices: adaptive farthest-reachable subgoal selection and the soft-horizon edge penalty both substantially outperform their alternatives.

Honest limitations section (Section 6) acknowledges dependence on base-learner reliability, dataset coverage, and distance-estimator accuracy; reproducibility details, hyperparameters, and per-agent distance mappings are provided in appendices.
weaknesses: Central claim of 'consistently improves or preserves performance' is not supported by the full results (Table 3): there are regressions (antmaze-giant-navigate QRL 11.8->10.8; humanoidmaze-giant-navigate GCIQL 0.7->0.5 and QRL 1.1->1.0; visual-humanoidmaze-medium-navigate HIQL 0.8->0.4) and many negligible changes (visual-antmaze-large-explore 0.0->0.8). Figure 3 selectively shows only the favorable tasks, and several reported gains are within error bars (e.g., antmaze-giant-navigate HIQL 65.0+/-4.1 vs 65.8+/-4.0).

Heavy hyperparameter sensitivity contradicts the 'lightweight and simple to adopt' narrative: Table 2 shows success swinging from 78.6 to 1.1 on antmaze-giant-stitch as tau/T vary, and Table 4 tunes tau and T separately per dataset and per base agent, which implies non-trivial per-task tuning.

Underperforms the GAS baseline on every antmaze task (e.g., antmaze-large-explore 26.6 vs 91.0; antmaze-giant-stitch 78.6 vs 86.2), and GAS is described as 'concurrent work' even though Baek et al. (ICML 2025) predates this submission; the head-to-head comparison is thus not in TTGS's favor on the harder locomotion domains.

Limited methodological novelty: test-time graph search over dataset/replay states with learned distances closely resembles Search on the Replay Buffer (Eysenbach et al., 2019), Sparse Graphical Memory (Emmons et al., 2020), Value Memory Graph (Zhu et al., 2023), and GAS (Baek et al., 2025); the main new element is applying it at inference time to offline GCRL with a value-derived distance.

No ablation isolating the graph/Dijkstra component itself: it is unclear whether the graph search adds value beyond simply decomposing into short value-based subgoals or random waypoints, so the source of the gains is not fully established.

Theoretical justification is thin: Dijkstra assumes additive edge costs, yet the value-derived distance need not satisfy the triangle inequality, and the superlinear penalty p(x)=x*1000^{x/tau} is heuristic with no analysis of when the resulting guide path is valid.

Presentation defects: the code link is broken ('Our code is available at .'), there are typos and citation errors ('antmaze-large-exlore-v0', 'Yin and Apter' for Yin & Abbeel, 'Wiliams'), and reference formatting is inconsistent.

strengths: Presents a simple, training-free inference-time planning wrapper for offline GCRL that requires no changes to training, no online interaction, and no privileged information.
Clear motivation: decomposes long-horizon goal reaching into short, reliable hops and provides illustrative examples (Figure 2) of base-policy failures and TTGS-guided subgoal selection.
Flexible framework: supports value-derived distances with closed-form mappings for common reward conventions and also accommodates domain-specific metrics.
Reports substantial gains on several OGBench long-horizon tasks, e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 0.0% -> 80.9% and GCIQL 0.0% -> 98.0%, and humanoidmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 4.4% -> 78.1%.
Ablations indicate that adaptive subgoal selection and edge-length penalties are important design choices, providing some practical insight.
Includes an honest limitations section acknowledging computational overhead and dependence on base-policy reliability and dataset coverage.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea of building a graph over dataset states, using a learned/value-based distance for edges, running shortest-path search, and executing subgoals with a frozen policy is closely related to prior work such as Search on the Replay Buffer (Eysenbach et al., 2019), Graph-Assisted Stitching (Baek et al., 2025), Value Memory Graph (Zhu et al., 2023), and Sparse Graphical Memory (Emmons et al., 2020). The main claimed distinction—training-free inference-time planning—is incremental, and the paper does not adequately compare against these test-time planners.

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity: Table 2 shows antmaze-giant-stitch HIQL performance ranging from 1.1% to 78.6% depending on τ and T, with similar sensitivity on pointmaze-giant-stitch. Hyperparameters are chosen per dataset and per base agent (Table 4), but the paper does not provide a principled selection procedure that avoids tuning on the evaluation tasks. This undermines the claim that TTGS is simple and reliable, and raises reproducibility concerns.

Unfair comparison to GAS: the authors state they ran GAS on all domains using antmaze hyperparameters (Appendix A). This likely disadvantages GAS on pointmaze and humanoidmaze, while on antmaze—where GAS was tuned—GAS outperforms TTGS (e.g., antmaze-giant-stitch GAS 86.2% vs HIQL+TTGS 78.6%; antmaze-large-explore GAS 91.0% vs 66.7%). Consequently, the claim that TTGS surpasses substantially more complex methods is not well supported.

Selective reporting in the main text: Figure 3 highlights only the largest stitching tasks where TTGS performs well, while the full Table 3 reveals many cases with no improvement or degradation (e.g., antmaze-giant-navigate HIQL 65.0% -> 65.8%, QRL 11.8% -> 10.8%; humanoidmaze-giant-navigate GCIQL 0.7% -> 0.5%; several visual-humanoidmaze tasks show no gains). Some gains have very high variance (antmaze-large-explore 26.6 ± 34.0), making claims of consistency questionable.

The central claim that policies fail to exploit geometric structure encoded in their value functions is not fully isolated. The domain-specific L2 distance often performs comparably to the value-derived distance (e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch: 83.0% L2 vs 80.9% value; antmaze-giant-stitch: 60.2% L2 vs 78.6% value), suggesting that much of the benefit may come from subgoal decomposition rather than value-function geometry specifically.

Reproducibility issues: the code link is blank ('Our code is available at .'), the website placeholder is empty, there is no sensitivity analysis for graph size M despite claiming M=100 can help, and the GAS training/tuning details are insufficient for reproduction.

Algorithm 1 contains errors and ambiguities (e.g., line 9 'g ← g'; subgoal variable conflated with the goal; candidate set construction depends on k and k_prev but is not clearly defined). The edge penalty p(x)=x·1000^{x/τ} is ad hoc and the constant 1000 is neither justified nor ablated.

The evaluation lacks comparisons to simple test-time baselines (e.g., random subgoal selection, nearest-neighbor subgoals, or SoRB-style planning with the same value function), so it is unclear how much of the gain is due to the specific TTGS design versus generic subgoal decomposition.

Presentation issues: multiple typos and inconsistencies ('exlore', 'Wiliams', 'Apter', inconsistent MDP/controlled Markov process terminology), low-quality figures, and unclear pseudocode reduce clarity.

strengths: The method is simple, training-free, and genuinely practical: TTGS is a plug-in test-time wrapper that requires no changes to training, no additional supervision, and no online interaction, which makes it easy to adopt with existing GCRL learners.

The empirical gains are substantial and often striking, e.g., HIQL improved from 0.0% to 80.9% on pointmaze-giant-stitch-v0 and from 4.4% to 78.1% on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch-v0, with consistent improvements across QRL, GCIQL, and HIQL on long-horizon locomotion.

The value-to-distance derivation is clean and principled: the closed-form mappings for sparse terminal reward and per-step penalty are correct, and reusing the learned goal-conditioned value function removes the need for handcrafted metrics.
The framework is flexible, demonstrated with both value-derived and simple domain-specific (body-position L2) distances, supporting the claim that it can accommodate any monotone distance signal.

The evaluation covers multiple OGBench domains (pointmaze, antmaze, humanoidmaze), dataset regimes (navigate/stitch/explore), and state-based as well as visual variants, with 50 rollouts per task and 8 seeds.

The paper is generally well written, with informative figures (motivation, distance fields, guide paths) and a clear algorithm description, plus hyperparameter and value-mapping details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited. Graph search over dataset/replay-buffer states with value-derived distances is conceptually close to prior work such as Search on the Replay Buffer (Eysenbach et al., 2019) and GAS (Baek et al., 2025); the main distinction (no training/online refinement) is incremental rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is a real concern. Both τ and T are tuned per dataset and per base agent (Appendix D), and Table 2 shows large swings in success rate as these vary (e.g., antmaze-giant-stitch drops from 78.6% at τ=12,T=24 to 19.0% at τ=24,T=48 to 1.1% at τ=48,T=96), which weakens the 'simple to adopt' claim.

Several headline results have very large variance (e.g., antmaze-large-explore HIQL+TTGS 26.6 ± 34.0; visual-antmaze-medium-explore 63.0 ± 28.1), making it difficult to judge reliability, and the paper does not report significance tests despite claiming consistent improvements.

The comparison against GAS and CompDiffuser is not apples-to-apples. The paper acknowledges these methods require extra training and different supervision, yet still frames TTGS as 'surpassing substantially more complex methods', which overstates the result since the base learners themselves were trained on the same data.

The central claim of identifying 'a specific cause of long-horizon failures' is overstated. The observation that policies degrade with horizon (Figure 2c) is well known, and the paper does not provide a mechanistic explanation for why value-derived distances encode reliable geometry beyond illustrative examples.

Missing ablations against simple alternatives. There is no comparison to planning with random/waypoint subgoals, to a purely Euclidean (no value function) distance at test time, or to the base policy given the true graph shortest path, which would isolate how much the value-derived distance contributes versus the graph-search wrapper itself.

There is no theoretical grounding for why the value-derived distance, which the authors admit may not satisfy metric axioms, produces reliable graph weights; the argument rests entirely on empirical reliability for nearby goals.

Presentation and polish issues: the code link is left blank ('Our code is available at .'), there are typos ('ef' at the end of an intro paragraph, 'Wiliams', 'apter', 'exlore' in tables), and the abstract/limitations underplay the dependence on base-learner competence (which the appendix results for weak base learners like visual-humanoidmaze confirm).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across five base learners (HIQL, QRL, GCIQL, SAW, OTA), multiple OGBench domains (pointmaze, antmaze, humanoidmaze, visual variants, manipulation), three data regimes, and 8 seeds with 50 rollouts per task, providing broad support for the method.

Large, practically meaningful gains on hard long-horizon locomotion tasks: e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 0.0→80.9, GCIQL 0.0→98.0; humanoidmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 4.4→78.1; antmaze-giant-stitch HIQL 1.4→78.6.

Simple, training-free test-time wrapper that requires no retraining, no online interaction, and adds modest overhead (graph construction 35–100 s once, shortest path usually <1 s per episode, ~1.5 ms per step), making it practical for frozen policies.

Novel soft-penalty edge-weight mechanism is well motivated and ablated: it preserves graph connectivity where hard thresholding fails, with disconnect ratios explaining the collapse on stitching tasks (e.g., antmaze-giant-stitch 78.6→2.2, humanoidmaze-giant-stitch 78.1→14.0).

Thorough empirical analysis: subgoal-selection ablation, soft vs. hard penalty, τ/T sensitivity, L2-kNN landmark baseline, triangle-inequality violations within the trust region, value-function geometry visualization, scaling with M, runtime breakdown, and replanning study.

Useful rollout-free diagnostic (largest hop ratio ρ) to predict when TTGS is likely to help, with a per-task table and an honest discussion of its necessary-but-not-sufficient nature (e.g., humanoidmaze-giant-stitch has low ρ but no GCIQL gain because the base policy is locally unreliable).

Honest limitations section and negative results: manipulation tasks show essentially no improvement, and the paper clearly states the three conditions under which TTGS helps (long-horizon stitching needed, locally reliable base policy, dataset coverage of intermediate states).

Reproducibility is generally well supported: public OGBench code and default hyperparameters for base learners, official code for SAW/OTA, an algorithm pseudocode, full hyperparameter table, and explicit value-to-distance mappings for each base learner.
weaknesses: Hyperparameter sensitivity is a serious practical concern: the edge threshold τ and subgoal budget T require per-environment/per-base-agent tuning. Table 3 shows HIQL+TTGS on antmaze-giant-stitch ranges from 1.1% to 78.6% depending on (τ,T), so the strong results depend on selecting the right regime. The paper uses a manual sweep and qualitative path inspection, which weakens the plug-and-play claim.

Methodological novelty is limited: graph search over offline dataset states with value-derived edge costs, Dijkstra planning, and subgoal selection overlaps substantially with prior work (e.g., SoRB, SGM, VMG, GSR). The soft penalty is a simple and effective modification, but the core recipe is not fundamentally new; the main contribution is an empirical re-evaluation plus this penalty.

Comparison fairness is not fully established: GAS and CompDiffuser numbers are taken from external papers/repositories rather than reproduced under identical conditions, and OGBench has random start/goal positions even for fixed task IDs and seeds. The paper does not include a direct test-time-only baseline from prior work, though it argues none exists.

Several results have very high variance and there are no formal significance tests. Examples include antmaze-large-explore HIQL+TTGS at 26.6 ± 34.0 and visual-antmaze-medium-explore at 63.0 ± 28.1; such variance makes claims of consistent improvement harder to evaluate.

The hop-ratio diagnostic relies on the same potentially miscalibrated value function used for planning and cannot capture local policy competence. The paper acknowledges it is necessary but not sufficient, so practitioners still need rollouts to confirm gains.

No theoretical guarantees are provided for the soft penalty, trust region, or value-to-distance mapping. The triangle-inequality analysis shows small local violations, but there is no bound on planning error or on how value-function noise propagates through shortest-path search.
The penalty function p(x)=x·1000^{x/τ} is arbitrary and is not ablated; sensitivity to the penalty shape, and to the number of graph vertices M beyond the reported sweep, remains unclear.

Minor algorithmic details are underspecified: Algorithm 1 does not state behavior when the projected start and goal vertices coincide or when no path exists in the graph, and projecting start/goal to nearest dataset vertices may introduce unquantified error in sparse graphs.

The manipulation results show essentially no improvement, which is honestly reported but limits the generality of the broad claim that existing GCRL policies can complete long-horizon tasks with a lightweight planning wrapper.

strengths: The core empirical result is compelling and well-supported: TTGS lifts frozen base policies from near-zero to >75-98% success on the hardest long-horizon stitching tasks (e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch 0.0->80.9 for HIQL, 0.0->98.0 for GCIQL; humanoidmaze-giant-stitch 4.4->78.1), and it is validated across five base learners (HIQL, GCIQL, QRL, SAW, OTA) rather than a single architecture, which strengthens generality claims.

The method is simple, training-free, and reproducible: it requires no parameter updates, no online interaction, and only <1 s per-episode planning plus ~1.5 ms per-step overhead. The paper provides full hyperparameters (Table 14), runtime breakdowns (Table 11), scaling sweeps (Table 12), and released code, which supports reproducibility.

The soft-penalty mechanism is the paper's most genuine technical contribution and is well justified by the soft-vs-hard ablation (Table 10) and the disconnect-ratio analysis: hard thresholding disconnects the graph on stitching tasks (e.g., antmaze-giant-stitch 78.6% -> 2.2%), whereas the soft penalty preserves connectivity. This is a non-obvious and practically useful finding.

The paper is unusually honest about the conditions under which it works. It explicitly characterizes the three preconditions (long-horizon stitching needed, locally reliable base policy, dataset coverage of intermediate states), reports the manipulation tasks where gains are 0-2 pp, and proposes the rollout-free hop-ratio diagnostic (Table 8) that cleanly separates the regimes where TTGS helps from those where it does not.

The supporting analyses are thorough and address plausible reviewer concerns: triangle-inequality violation statistics within the trust region (Table 6), an L2-kNN landmark baseline with a full per-k sweep (Table 7), clustering-based vertex selection (Table 9), replanning (Table 13), and a fixed-hyperparameter cross-domain comparison against GAS (Table 5).

The value-to-distance derivations (Section 3.1, Appendix B) are correct for the stated reward conventions and generalize to QRL's quasi-metric head and OTA's multi-resolution critics, showing the framework is not overfit to a single reward convention.
weaknesses: Originality is thin relative to ICML's bar. The core recipe - build a graph over data, assign value-derived edge costs, run Dijkstra, and feed subgoals to a frozen policy - is essentially SoRB (Eysenbach et al., 2019) executed offline at test time. The delta over prior graph-search GCRL is the soft penalty (an exponential p(x)=x*1000^{x/tau}) plus the offline/test-time setting. The claim of being 'the first method that operates purely offline and at test time' is overstated, since VMG (Zhu et al., 2023) already performs offline graph-MDP construction and subgoal feeding; the distinction is largely a matter of framing.

The 'training-free / negligible tuning' framing is partially contradicted by the experiments. Table 14 shows tau and T are tuned per dataset and per base learner (values range over (6,12) to (48,96)), and Appendix L admits 1-2 settings were tried per dataset/agent with manual inspection of shortest paths. This is genuine per-task hyperparameter engineering, which weakens the central lightweight-deployment narrative.

The claim that TTGS 'improves or maintains success' is not fully accurate. Several entries regress: QRL antmaze-medium-stitch 62.0->40.1, HIQL humanoidmaze-medium-stitch 86.1->84.6, QRL humanoidmaze-medium-stitch 19.4->14.4, GCIQL humanoidmaze-giant-navigate 0.7->0.5. These regressions are not discussed, and a mechanism for when TTGS hurts (rather than defaults to base behavior) is missing, despite the paper's strong 'does not degrade performance' claim.

Statistical reliability is a concern on several key tasks. Variances are large (e.g., antmaze-large-explore 26.6 +/- 34.0; visual-antmaze-medium-explore 63.0 +/- 28.1; humanoidmaze-giant-stitch with L2 74.2 +/- 17.5), and no significance testing is reported. Some headline gains on individual tasks may not be statistically distinguishable from the base policy given the reported standard deviations and 8-seed protocol.

The hop-ratio diagnostic is acknowledged to be necessary-but-not-sufficient, and the counterexample (humanoidmaze-giant-stitch, rho=0.112, gain 0.0) is precisely the case where a rollout-free predictor would be most valuable. As presented, the diagnostic requires knowing local policy competence, which itself needs rollouts, limiting its practical value relative to simply running TTGS.

The theoretical framing is asserted rather than demonstrated. The claim that value functions 'encode locally consistent geometric structure sufficient for planning' rests on empirical triangle-inequality statistics (Table 6) rather than any analysis of why this structure emerges or when it fails; the average violation of 0.002-3.1 steps is reported without a link to planning error bounds or success probability.

The manipulation evaluation uses only GCIQL, whereas the locomotion evaluation uses five base learners. The negative result (no gains on manipulation) is therefore supported by a much narrower evidence base than the positive result, making the 'conditions under which TTGS helps' argument less balanced than presented.

strengths: The paper addresses a significant problem in offline GCRL: long-horizon tasks where base policies fail. The proposed TTGS is a simple, training-free wrapper that requires no additional supervision or online interaction, making it highly practical.

The soft-penalty mechanism for edge weights is a novel and well-motivated solution to the problem of unreliable value estimates creating wormholes in the graph. The ablation study convincingly shows that the soft penalty outperforms both no penalty and hard thresholding, especially on stitching tasks where connectivity is crucial.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing. TTGS is tested with five base learners (HIQL, QRL, GCIQL, SAW, OTA) across multiple domains (pointmaze, antmaze, humanoidmaze), including state-based and pixel-based observations, and three data regimes. The gains on long-horizon locomotion are substantial, e.g., pointmaze-giant-stitch HIQL from 0.0% to 80.9% and GCIQL from 0.0% to 98.0%.

The paper provides thorough ablations and analyses, including adaptive subgoal selection vs. next-subgoal, hyperparameter sensitivity, scaling with number of vertices M, replanning effects, triangle-inequality violation statistics, and runtime breakdown. This level of detail supports the claims and aids reproducibility.

The hop-ratio diagnostic is a useful, rollout-free tool to predict whether TTGS will help on a new task, with empirical validation showing it separates locomotion (low ratio) from manipulation (high ratio) tasks.

The limitations section is honest and comprehensive, discussing conditions for success, dataset access, failure modes, and future directions. The negative results on manipulation are explained via value-function geometry visualizations, which is a responsible treatment of negative results.

The comparison to training-based methods (GAS, CompDiffuser) is framed appropriately as TTGS operating under stricter constraints, and the fixed-hyperparameter cross-domain comparison demonstrates robustness.
Reproducibility is well addressed: code and videos are promised, hyperparameters are listed in detail, runtime is measured, and value-to-distance mappings for each base learner are provided.
weaknesses: The core idea of building a graph over dataset states and using value-derived distances for planning is closely related to prior work such as SoRB (Eysenbach et al., 2019) and SGM (Emmons et al., 2020). The novelty lies mainly in the test-time-only setting and the soft penalty, which may be seen as an incremental contribution.

The method requires per-environment tuning of hyperparameters τ and T, as evidenced by Table 14. Although the paper provides guidance and a diagnostic, it is not fully hyperparameter-free, which may hinder adoption in new domains.

The soft-penalty function p(x) = x * 1000^{x/τ} includes an arbitrary constant (1000) that is not justified or ablated. The sensitivity of performance to the exact form of the penalty is not explored.

The comparison with GAS and CompDiffuser is not perfectly controlled because those methods train additional components, while TTGS relies on a pretrained value function and policy. The paper acknowledges this, but a direct test-time-only baseline (e.g., greedy value-based subgoal selection without graph search) is missing.
The hop-ratio diagnostic is necessary but not sufficient, as the paper itself notes. Its computation depends on the chosen τ, and the sensitivity of ρ to τ is not analyzed.

The method's effectiveness is highly dependent on dataset coverage and base policy local reliability, which limits its applicability. For example, on manipulation tasks TTGS yields no improvement, and on humanoidmaze-giant-stitch with GCIQL, low hop ratio does not translate to gains because the base policy is unreliable at short range.

The value-to-distance mappings are specific to the reward conventions of the evaluated base learners. For new base learners, users must derive the mapping, which may be a practical barrier and could introduce errors if the reward convention is unknown or different.

Some results exhibit high variance (e.g., antmaze-large-explore HIQL+TTGS 26.6 ± 34.0), suggesting instability. Although the paper attributes this to random start/goal positions, the evaluation uses only 50 rollouts per task; increasing the number of rollouts or seeds could strengthen the evidence.

The claim of 'negligible computational overhead' should be qualified: graph construction takes 35–100 seconds one-time, and per-episode planning takes up to ~1 second. While small relative to training, this may not be negligible for real-time or resource-constrained deployment.

The paper does not provide a quantitative analysis of how well value-derived distances correlate with true step distances locally, beyond triangle-inequality violation statistics. A direct correlation analysis would more directly support the central claim that value functions encode locally consistent geometric structure.
